resources.string: Results are for casual reference only, not for professional engineering

Disclaimer: All calculation results in this app are generated from simplified mechanical models and representative material values. They are for rough reference in everyday scenarios only and cannot replace professional engineering analysis. For any matter involving personal safety, structural safety, or significant property safety, please consult a professional engineer. All consequences arising from the use of this app are borne by the user.

Safety factor %1$s is below 1.0: member stress exceeds the material strength representative value. In actual use it will visibly bend or even break. Reduce load, thicken the section, or use stronger material and recompute.
Safety factor %1$s is below 2.0: deflection may be large under normal use, and risk is higher with material flaws or long-term loading. Reduce load or enlarge section for margin.
Bending stress exceeded: transverse cracks first appear on the tension side at mid-span, then obvious sagging or fracture.
Compression capacity exceeded: buckling or local instability first, then sudden collapse (not gradual bending).
Axial stress exceeded: tension side cracks, compression side crushes.
Reduce load: current load is %1$s× capacity. For safety margin (factor 1.5), reduce to about %2$s%% of current.
Thicken section: increase bending height from %1$s to about %2$s (section %3$s → %4$s), stress drops to 1/%5$s.
Thickening alone is impractical: to bring stress back to safe range, section height needs to be about %1$s× (%2$s → %3$s). Better change the structural form.
Change structural form: add intermediate posts/supports or diagonal bracing. Bending moment drops roughly with the square of span (halve span, moment drops to ~1/4).
Use stronger material (e.g. pine → birch, aluminum → steel), or reduce span and recompute.
The deformation magnitude is small. You can get an intuitive feel from the max deflection value.

resources.string: Simplify the problem into a constant-thickness, flat-bottom thin-wall vessel: four-node shell elements (MITC4) compute wall displacement and stress under fill pressure and self-weight, showing wall bulging and bottom-corner stress concentration. Loads (hydrostatic / granular lateral / self-weight) are generated automatically from the fill. Confirm to solve.
Engineering-formula estimate · linear elastic · conservative; not a formal design
Deformed elliptical ring (dashed = original circle; deflection amplified)
Defaults & assumptions (defaults apply to inputs not provided):
This is an engineering-formula estimate that ignores beneficial soil-spring and cover restraint, so it is conservative; formal design should follow codes and site investigation.
Compute: 4-node shell (MITC4) displacement/stress field + tension/compression strength checks; loads generated from the fill (hydrostatic / granular lateral / floor reaction / self-weight)

Note: shell elements apply to constant-thickness, flat-bottom, vertical vessels; the floor is rigidly connected to the wall (stress concentration shows at the corner). No roof, openings, stiffeners or hopper details.
Thin-wall vessels (MITC4 shells) are more expensive than beam elements. Large vessels or fine meshes may take seconds to ~tens of seconds; use a coarser level if the phone lags.
Fine/ultra mesh: many shell elements, solving may take ~tens of seconds or more and use a lot of memory. For a quick estimate on an average phone, use medium or coarse.
